Appeal
ap-pēl'
v. and n. (to remove a cause to a higher court; Paul's use of Roman citizenship to reach Caesar's judgment seat)
Latin appellare, to call upon or address. In Roman law the provocatio ad Caesarem was the citizen's right to have his case transferred out of a provincial court to the emperor — a right Paul possessed by birth and used deliberately.

Biblical Definition

Standing before Festus, with a proposal on the table to move his trial to Jerusalem where an ambush was waiting, Paul said: “I stand at Caesar's judgment seat, where I ought to be judged: to the Jews have I done no wrong, as thou very well knowest” (Acts 25:10), and then: “if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar” (Acts 25:11). Festus consulted his council and answered, “Hast thou appealed unto Caesar? unto Caesar shalt thou go” (Acts 25:12). The appeal was irreversible, and Agrippa afterwards observed as much: “This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Caesar” (Acts 26:32). Paul explained his reasoning later in Rome without bitterness: “when the Jews spake against it, I was constrained to appeal unto Caesar; not that I had ought to accuse my nation of” (Acts 28:19). It was the appeal that carried the gospel to Rome at imperial expense, and Paul had long said he must see Rome. He used a legal right, and God used it to fulfil a purpose stated chapters earlier.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines appeal as to remove a cause from an inferior to a superior judge or court, and notes the practice among the Romans of appealing to the emperor.

expand to see more

APPEAL, v.i. To refer to a superior judge or court, for the decision of a cause depending.

2. To refer to another for the decision of a question controverted.

APPEAL, n. The removal of a cause or suit from an inferior to a superior tribunal.

2. In the ancient Roman government, an appeal to the emperor, as the last resort.

TRIBUNAL, n. The seat of a judge; the bench on which a judge and his associates sit for administering justice.

Key Scripture

Acts 25:11 — "For if I be an offender, or have committed any thing worthy of death, I refuse not to die: but if there be none of these things whereof these accuse me, no man may deliver me unto them. I appeal unto Caesar."

Acts 25:12 — "Then Festus, when he had conferred with the council, answered, Hast thou appealed unto Caesar? unto Caesar shalt thou go."

Acts 26:32 — "Then said Agrippa unto Festus, This man might have been set at liberty, if he had not appealed unto Caesar."

Acts 28:19 — "But when the Jews spake against it, I was constrained to appeal unto Caesar; not that I had ought to accuse my nation of."

Modern Corruption

Using lawful protections is treated as a failure of faith, and Paul used every one available to him without apology.

expand to see more

A certain piety holds that a Christian under unjust treatment should simply submit and say nothing — that invoking a legal right shows a want of trust. Paul's conduct refutes it repeatedly. He appealed to Caesar; he told the magistrates at Philippi to come and fetch him out themselves; he informed the centurion at Jerusalem that he was a Roman before the scourging began. He also submitted to imprisonment, beating and death when the protections ran out. The two are not in tension: providence works through means, and a citizen's legal standing is one of the means God has provided. Paul used them, and when they failed he suffered without complaint.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereignty visible in the outcome. Agrippa's remark that Paul could have been freed if he had not appealed reads like a lament over a tactical blunder, and Luke records it deadpan at the end of the chapter. But the Lord had stood by Paul in Jerusalem and told him he must bear witness at Rome, and the appeal is what carried him there — escorted, fed and guarded at the empire's expense, to preach in his own hired house with no man forbidding him. What looked like a lost acquittal was the road to the commission. Providence commonly works this way, and it is usually only visible afterwards.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek epikaleomai (G1941), to call upon, to appeal — Acts 25:11, 25:12, 25:21, 25:25, 26:32, 28:19; bema (G968), a judgment seat — Acts 25:10.

expand to see more

Greek epikaleomai (G1941) — to call upon; in the middle voice, to appeal to a higher court; six times in Acts 25-28.

Greek bema (G968) — a raised place, a judgment seat; Acts 25:10, and 2 Corinthians 5:10 of the judgment seat of Christ.

Greek Sebastos (G4575) — Augustus, the imperial title; Acts 25:21, 25:25.

Latin provocatio — the Roman citizen's right of appeal to the emperor, which Paul held from birth.

Acts 23:11 gives the promise the appeal served: as thou hast testified of me in Jerusalem, so must thou bear witness also at Rome.

Usage

"“I appeal unto Caesar” — a legal right, used deliberately."

"“Hast thou appealed unto Caesar? unto Caesar shalt thou go” — and it could not be undone."

"“This man might have been set at liberty” — and would not have reached Rome."
